o: The qualifications of a faithful pastor.
The evil temper and practices of false teachers.
bg: Was probably written about the same time as the first epistle to Timothy, with which it has many affinities. "Both letters were addressed to persons left by the writer to preside in their respective churches during his absence.
Now called Candia, one of the largest islands in the Meditterranean, about 140 miles long and 35 broad. It was at one time a very prosperous and populous island, having a "hundred cities."

Honourable, was with Paul and Barnabas at Antioch, and accompanied them to the council at Jerusalem (Gal. 2:1-3; Acts 15:2), although his name nowhere occurs in the Acts of the Apostles. He appears to have been a Gentile, and to have been chiefly engaged in ministering to Gentiles; for Paul sternly refused to have him circumcised, inasmuch as in his case the cause of gospel liberty was at stake.
ch.s: This chapter covers: The apostle salutes Titus (vv. 1–4); The qualifications of a faithful pastor (vv. 5–9); The evil temper and practices of false teachers (vv. 10–16). People named: Paul, Titus. Places: Crete.
ch.mh: All are the servants of God who are not slaves of sin and Satan.
q: Read verses 1–4 (The apostle salutes Titus). What is happening, and what stands out to you most?
In verses 5–9 (The qualifications of a faithful pastor), what do you learn about faith and trust?
Verse 2 is one of the most cross-referenced verses in this chapter. Read it alongside Numbers 23:19. How do the two passages shed light on each other?
What does Paul’s part in this chapter teach you — as an example to follow or a warning to heed?
Where do you see the theme of grace and mercy in this chapter, and how does it connect to the rest of Titus?
What is one specific way you can put this chapter into practice this week?
ch.aq: See the miserable state of hypocrites, such as have a form of godliness, but are without the power; yet let us not be so ready to fix this charge on others, as careful that it does not apply to ourselves.
ch.a: Name one worry and deliberately hand it over to God in prayer each day this week.

o: The duties which become sound doctrine.
All is enforced from the holy design of the gospel, which concerns all believers.
bg: Was probably written about the same time as the first epistle to Timothy, with which it has many affinities. "Both letters were addressed to persons left by the writer to preside in their respective churches during his absence.
ch.s: This chapter covers: The duties which become sound doctrine (vv. 1–8); Believing servants must be obedient (vv. 9,10); All is enforced from the holy design of the gospel, which concerns all believers (vv. 11–15).
ch.mh: Old disciples of Christ must behave in every thing agreeably to the Christian doctrine.
q: Read verses 1–8 (The duties which become sound doctrine). What is happening, and what stands out to you most?
In verses 9,10 (Believing servants must be obedient), what do you learn about salvation and redemption?
Verse 14 is one of the most cross-referenced verses in this chapter. Read it alongside Hebrews 9:14. How do the two passages shed light on each other?
Where do you see the theme of love in this chapter, and how does it connect to the rest of Titus?
What is one specific way you can put this chapter into practice this week?
ch.aq: Let us inquire whether our whole dependence is placed upon that grace which saves the lost, pardons the guilty, and sanctifies the unclean.
ch.a: Thank God for His deliverance, and share what He has done for you with one person.

o: Obedience to magistrates, and becoming behaviour towards all, are enforced from what believers were before conversion, and what they are made, through Christ.
Good works to be done, and useless disputes avoided.
bg: Was probably written about the same time as the first epistle to Timothy, with which it has many affinities. "Both letters were addressed to persons left by the writer to preside in their respective churches during his absence.
City of victory, where Paul intended to winter (Titus 3:12). There were several cities of this name.
In New Testament times, was a Roman province lying north of Greece. It was governed by a propraetor with the title of proconsul.
(gift of Artemis), a companion of St. Paul. (Titus 3:12) According to tradition he was bishop of Lystra.
ch.s: This chapter covers: Obedience to magistrates, and becoming behaviour towards all, are enforced from what believers were before conversion, and what they are made, through Christ (vv. 1–7); Good works to be done, and useless disputes avoided (vv. 8–11); Directions and exhortations (vv. 12–15). People named: Artemas, Tychicus, Zenas, Apollos, Titus. Places: Nicopolis, Macedonia.
ch.mh: Spiritual privileges do not make void or weaken, but confirm civil duties.
q: Read verses 1–7 (Obedience to magistrates, and becoming behaviour towards all, are enforced from what believers were before conversion, and what they are made, through Christ). What is happening, and what stands out to you most?
In verses 8–11 (Good works to be done, and useless disputes avoided), what do you learn about grace and mercy?
Verse 5 is one of the most cross-referenced verses in this chapter. Read it alongside Ephesians 2:8–9. How do the two passages shed light on each other?
What does Artemas’s part in this chapter teach you — as an example to follow or a warning to heed?
Where do you see the theme of salvation and redemption in this chapter, and how does it connect to the rest of Titus?
What is one specific way you can put this chapter into practice this week?
ch.aq: Though we may now think some sins light and little, if the Lord awaken the conscience, we shall feel even the smallest sin heavy upon our souls.
ch.a: Show the same mercy you have received to someone who does not deserve it.
